segments.text: We turn now to Paul's letter to the Philippians and chapter 1.
The letter to the Philippians, chapter 1, beginning at verse 1.
Paul and Timothy, bond servants of Christ Jesus to all the saints in Christ Jesus who
are in Philippi, including the overseers and deacons.
Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
I thank my God in all my remembrance of you, always offering prayer with joy in my every
prayer for you all, in view of your participation in the gospel from the first day until now.
Paul's letter to the Philippians is a letter that speaks much about the subject of Christian
joy and many other truths concerning the deity and the humanity of Christ and Paul's own pursuit
after godliness.
And there are many precious lessons that we can learn from this letter.
Paul himself had established this church in Philippi and it was the place where the Christians
at Philippi had heard of his rejoicing in the jail when he had been beaten up and locked
up.
And so when he spoke about joy, it was from a very meaningful position.
He himself, when he wrote this letter, was in a prison in Rome awaiting his sentence.
And so it was not an armchair theologian speaking about joy, but an apostle who was in prison
suffering for the gospel's sake and thereby proving that Christian joy is something that
is not altered by circumstances.
And he speaks much about joy in this letter.
In fact, it's one of the key words which occurs quite often in this letter.
And we see here Paul and Timothy, he includes Timothy in writing this letter, Bond's Servants
of Christ Jesus.
Now there's a difference between a bond servant and a servant.
A bond servant is a slave and that's what Paul always considered himself to be.
A servant is one who works for wages, one who has rights, who can take leave and who
can work for certain hours, and then who is free to do what he likes, who probably
has his own home and his own family, but comes to work for wages.
But a bond servant is a slave who has given up all his rights, who has been bought by
his master, and who has no more rights on himself.
He has no right to ask for payment or salary or free time or privileged leave or anything.
And that's what Paul considered himself.
And all those who worked with Paul considered themselves like this.
Paul and Timothy, bond servants of Christ Jesus.
In other words, they had given themselves over to Christ without any rights.
They didn't expect the Lord to do anything for them, though the Lord did much for them.
But they did not expect anything.
So many Christians are disappointed in their progress because they are not bond servants.
They serve God and then they wonder, now what will I get for this servant?
Now such is not a bond servant.
Such is a servant who is working for wages.
And a lot of our joy can be removed if we work for wages or if we work for any other
type of reward.
True joy can come only when we surrender ourselves to the Lord to be his slaves.
And this is a question that you could ask yourself.
Are you a slave of Christ or a servant?
Are you one who feels you still have certain rights over your life?
How you can spend your time and your money?
And you are perhaps a servant, but not a slave.
A slave is one who realizes he's lost all rights over his life.
His money is not his, his time is not his, his body is not his, there's nothing which
belongs to him.
And it's only such that can have an effective ministry in the church.
Paul and Timothy bond servants of Christ Jesus to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are
in Philippi.
And the Christians here are called saints, which refers to holiness or character being
set apart from the world, for the word saint means one who is set apart, set apart from
the world to be God's exclusively.
And these Christians in Philippi, Paul calls them saints, which refers to the primary aspect
of our calling in Christ is to be holy.
God has chosen us not primarily to go to heaven, but that we might be holy and blameless
before him in love.
We read in Ephesians chapter 1 and verse 4 that he chose us in Christ before the foundation
of the world that we should be holy and blameless before him.
Why did God choose us?
Not that we might go to heaven, but primarily that we might be holy and blameless before
him.
And that's why when we are called saints, that refers to the primary aspect of our
calling, that we might be set apart from the world and from the flesh and from all
that is unlike God and contrary to God's will in this world, that we might be set apart
for him.
And so the word saints is another word that refers to us, that we need to understand.
Saints in Christ Jesus who are in Philippi, including the overseers and deacons.
The overseers and deacons were the leaders of the church.
The overseers were the elders.
Now that word overseer has been translated in some other places as bishop and it's the
same function which in other places is described as elders.
So in the New Testament, whenever you read the word overseer or bishop or elder, they
mean basically the same thing.
And there was never just one elder or overseer in a church, there was always more than one.
The leadership of the early church was always in the hands of more than one.
A group of elders, at least two, but always in the plural.
And so he says to the overseers, those who are elders, those who are bishops, or those
who are overseers.
In other words, those, not those who have an office, probably these people were secular
men.
We shouldn't think of these people as those who had got into full-time Christian work.
In the first century, the overseers of bishops or elders were most of them people
in some secular occupation who were giving spiritual leadership to the local church.
And that is a function that we need to have once again today.
In the early church, there were no pastors.
One pastor looking after church was completely unheard of in the early church.
And a bishop, such as we know today, was totally unheard of in the first century.
These are all things that man's traditions brought into the church subsequently.
In the early church, the leadership of the church were in the hands of men, almost all
of them in a secular occupation, who were called elders.
And there were deacons.
And the deacons were those who looked after the material aspect of things more in the
local church, and who, through faithful in it, probably later, became elders.
But initially began with the material, the practical responsibilities, such as the distribution
of food we read off in Acts chapter 6, where seven deacons were chosen.
And they were servants, looking after the practical aspect of the local church.
So there's much that we can learn from that first verse from these four words, bond
servants, saints, overseers, and deacons.
And Paul writes to these and says, grace to you, and peace from God our Father and the
Lord Jesus Christ.
There's never a time in our life when we don't need to receive more grace, more grace
from God, so that we can partake more of His nature and more of the fullness of God
that there is in Christ.
And peace, this is something that we need to receive continuously from God, to keep our
hearts and minds in peace.
He speaks more of that in Philippians 4, verse 6 and 7.
And these were two words that Paul loved to use whenever he wrote to the Christians that
grace and peace might be their portion at all times.
And he says further in verse 3, I thank my God in all my remembrance of you.
Here's another thing that was characteristic of Paul in all his letters.
Whenever you read any of the letters, Corinthians and Ephesians and Philippians, you find him
saying, I thank my God for you people.
Even to the Corinthians, this is the most amazing thing.
To a carnal group of Christians in Corinth, he could say in 1 Corinthians in chapter
1, I thank God always concerning you, 1 Corinthians 1.4, for the grace that was given you in
Christ Jesus.
He did go on to reprove them for their wrong, but he first of all began by thanking God
for them and appreciating all that was good in them.
And he praised God for that.
And that's a good habit for us to develop as we look at others.
Our natures are basically critical of others.
We tend to find the faults in others more than the good points.
But we need to begin where the Apostle began in all his letters to learn to thank God
for the good things that we see in one another.
And that will make a tremendous difference in our own state of Christian joy welling
up in our heart.
We turn now to Philippians in chapter 1 and verse 3.
I thank my God in all my remembrance of you, always offering prayer with joy in my every
prayer for you all, in view of your participation in the gospel from the first day until now.
For I am confident of this very thing that he who began a good work in you will perfect
it until the day of Christ Jesus.
For it is only right for me to feel this way about you all because I have you in my
heart since both in my imprisonment and in the defense and confirmation of the gospel
you all are partakers of grace with me.
Now we saw last week something about the first three verses and I mentioned how Paul
always began a letter, usually anyway, by thanking God for these Christians to whom
he was writing and telling them how he was thanking God for them.
Not just when he wrote that letter, but he says here I thank my God in all my remembrance
of you, always offering prayer with joy in my every prayer for you all.
Now when we live according to the flesh, we find that it's far easier to find faults
in others that we can criticize rather than things that we can thank God for.
One of the marks of a spiritual man is that he finds something in other children of God
that he can thank God for.
He is not perpetually critical of everything, but he sees something that he can thank God
for.
But he doesn't shut his eyes and live in a world of unreality, imagining that there's
nothing wrong, but he does thank God for what is good.
And if he would only develop this habit, there would be far more joy in our own lives,
far more peace in our relationships with one another, in our homes, as husbands and wives.
If you learn to thank God for the good things we see in one another, and as brothers and
sisters in a local church, if you learn to thank God for one another and thank God for
the work that God is doing in others, here is a habit that's almost seldom found
in Christians at all.
Very rarely do we find a Christian who has this habit to examine yourself.
How much have you thanked God for those in your own home, your marriage partner, your
children, or those in your church, your spiritual leaders and your brothers and sisters?
And then we shall discover basically how unthankful we are.
And here is the cause for a lot of our own misery and problems, because the Spirit wants
to make us a joyful people, thanking God at every remembrance of our fellow brothers and
sisters in Christ, always offering prayer with joy in my every prayer for you all.
Whenever Paul prayed, it was with joy for these Christians.
One reason was that it was going well with them, with most of them anyway.
It was going well.
They were growing spiritually.
And so in every prayer for them, he says, I give thanks and I pray with joy.
And here with a particular reason in mind, in view of your participation in the gospel
from the first day until now, they shared with Paul in his preaching of the gospel.
In other words, they prayed for him and they supported him.
We read in Philippians in chapter four, verse 18, about the gift of money that they had
sent Paul in his need and when he was in prison and which he received.
Now most of the time, the Apostle Paul supported himself.
Obviously, he couldn't do that when he was in prison.
But when he was in Corinth or in Ephesus or in Thessalonica, most places he would work
with his own hands and support himself as a tentmaker so that he would not be chargeable
to any of the saints, thereby setting them an example to make the gospel free of charge
to all, showing them that it is more blessed to give and not to seek to receive.
But when he was in prison, the Philippian Christians sent him a gift and he received
it.
And he was thankful for their sharing with him in the spreading of the gospel, not
only through money, but by praying for him, no doubt, and in cooperating with him in
the spread of the gospel in those parts.
And from the first day until now, he says, you have shared with me in the preaching of the
gospel and I thank God for you people.
And he goes on to say further in verse six, I'm confident of this very thing, that he
who began a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Christ Jesus.
Paul was not a pessimist, always looking at the dark side of things and thinking
how miserable a lot of Christians were.
He looked at those good things and he looked at the work which God had begun in the
Christians in Philippi and he says, I believe that what God has begun, he's going to
complete, he will complete it.
Of course, it doesn't mean that God can automatically complete it without any
cooperation from the parties of Philippian Christians.
What he was saying here included his confidence that the Philippian Christians would respond
to God in such a way that God would be able to complete the good work that he had
begun.
And so he says, I'm confident.
That was a confidence not only in God, but also in the fact that he believed that the
Philippian Christians would respond in submission, in faith, and in obedience to God,
so that God could complete the work he had begun.
And so he says, I believe that he will perfect it till the time it's completed and
perfected and we are made like Christ Jesus.
The Holy Spirit continues to work in us until the day of Christ Jesus, to make us like Him.
And here is where we are to yield in cooperation to the Holy Spirit's working in submission
without any complaining, in yielding our will, denying ourselves.
And this is where people should have confidence.
God should have the confidence.
The spiritual leaders should have the confidence in us that we are of that type, submitted to
the Spirit that that work which God has begun will be completed in us in the day of Christ
Jesus.
And he says, for it's only right for me to feel this way about you all, because I have
you in my heart.
The Apostle Paul bore the churches he had founded in his heart.
That's why God had a message through him for them.
If we are to have a message for the church, we have to bear them in our heart.
This is the secret of having a word from the Lord for those for whom God has given us
a spiritual responsibility.
If you are a spiritual leader or if you're called a minister to the word to a group
of Christians for whom you have responsibility, God can give you a right word only if you
bear them in your heart.
Only if you can say like Paul could say, I have you in my heart.
And where we bear other Christians in our heart, we shall not find it easy to criticize
them or to scold them or to beat them as it were when we preached to them.
But we shall seek to give to them that word which God has given to our heart for them
because we bear them in our hearts.
Now, it's very important for us to remember, particularly those who minister the word,
that it is not by study, it's not by preparing messages in our study that we have the right
word, but by bearing Christians in our heart and having a concern for them.
And that's what Paul had, a real genuine concern.
He says in 2 Corinthians and chapter 11 about how the care of all the churches came upon
him.
And this was something that was true of the apostles.
In Corinthians 11, 28, the daily pressure, he says, of the concern for all the churches.
Paul carried a daily pressure upon his heart of a concern for all the churches he had established
and the Christians in these churches.
And therefore he would pray for them.
And therefore he had a right word for them in each occasion.
It's only right for me to feel this way about you, he says in Philippians 1, 7,
because I have you in my heart since both in my imprisonment and in the defense and
the confirmation of the gospel, you all are partakers of grace with me.
There is a grace that Paul had been made a partaker of.
He had come into the new covenant and experienced the grace of God through the Holy Spirit.
And he says, you have become partakers with me of that same grace, that grace that led
Paul into a life of victory over sin.
And as the Philippian Christians partook of it, they came into a life of victory too.
And in Paul's imprisonment and suffering for the gospel's sake, also they were willing to
take their share of suffering and stand by him and not forsaken like so many other Christians
had done.
And God is my witness, he says, how I long for you all with the affection of Christ
Jesus.
Here is another expression of Paul's great longing for these Christians in Philippi.
Paul was not a professional evangelist or preacher.
He was a father, and all the people whom he brought to the Lord were just like his own
children.
He went away from them, he couldn't forget about them.
The professional preacher preaches, collects his offerings, and goes away, and he couldn't
care less for the people he is converted or preached to.
Paul could never be like that.
And the great need of the hour is for more people like Paul, who can say to Christians,
I have you in my heart, and I long for you all with the affection of Christ Jesus.
It is only through such people that even today the church can be established just like it was
in the days of the apostles.
We turn now to Philippians chapter one and verse nine.
Last week we saw something about the concern that Paul had for the Christians in Philippi,
how he bore them in his heart, as he says in verse seven, and how he longed after them
with the affection of Christ Jesus.
Actually Paul was a faithful minister of the gospel, and he prayed for these Christians.
He says, this I pray that your love may abound still more and more in real knowledge and
all discernment.
Paul's main prayer for the Christians in most places was that they would abound in
love for one another, and this is something that we need to pray for even today, for
the Christians among whom we are found.
For there is a great need all over the world for Christians to have a fervent love for
one another.
Jesus said, by this shall all men know you are my disciples, when you love one another.
That's very interesting to think of that.
Jesus did not say that the world would know that we are his disciples when we love the
people in the world.
God so loved the world, and we're to love the people in the world too.
But Jesus said the world would know that we are his disciples when they see our love
for one another.
And so Paul prayed that the love of these Philippian Christians for one another would
abound still more and more, but not this human, soulish type of love which does not
love the truth and which is more like a buddy-buddy relationship that people have.
No, here is a love that grows more and more in real knowledge and all discernment so
that you may approve the things that are excellent, so that you may distinguish between
the things which differ, it says in the margin of my Bible, in order to be sincere
and blameless until the day of Christ.
It's not a love that shuts our eyes to unrighteousness in our brother.
It's a love that does not rejoice in unrighteousness, as we read in 1 Corinthians 13, but rejoices
in the truth, and therefore longs that our brother will go to all that is highest in
godliness that God has prepared for him.
So it is that type of a love, the type of a love that can rebuke like Jesus loves,
whomsoever I love, I rebuke, he says in Revelation 3.
It's a love that can rebuke because it seeks the highest good of the other, but it's
a love that bears the other person in your heart and has a concern for him and is
interested in his spiritual welfare and physical and material welfare.
And he says, I pray that this type of love may abound in all knowledge and in all
discernment so that you may distinguish between the things that differ.
In other words, if we are to love one another with the love of God, it's important that
we grow in holiness too.
We cannot increase in love if we are not growing in purity, otherwise our love will
be an impure type of love.
Now there's a lot of human love, some of it which is very good, like a mother's love
for a child.
But it is not divine love.
Divine love is superior to the love of her mother for a child because her mother very
often overlooks the weaknesses in her child and she very often cannot believe that her
children can ever do anything wrong.
She stands by her children through thick and thin, irrespective of whether they have
done right or wrong.
Now God, it says, is opposed to the proud, and one of his own children, if they are
proud, God will oppose him.
So God's love is not something that stands by us through thick and thin, irrespective
of our own spiritual condition.
It's a love that seeks our highest good, and so if we are lifted up in
pride he will oppose us so that he might humble us, so that he might do us good.
And so the prayer of Paul here is that we might grow in real knowledge, in a real
knowledge of God, and in discernment concerning what is human and what is divine.
The great need for discernment is in the area of what is nearly human, which comes
out from the human soul and what is inspired by the Holy Spirit.
He says, so that you may be able to distinguish between the things that differ or
approve the things that are excellent.
In other words, so that you may choose the things that are excellent above the
things that are merely good.
There are many things that are good, but we are to reject them so that we might
choose the things that are excellent.
And that's what he means here.
It's not just a question of giving up hatred, but it's also a question of giving
up that type of love which is merely soulish and human, and partaking of the
love of God through the Holy Spirit, so that we love others wisely.
There's a lot of unwise love, even among Christians, particularly when it comes
to our own flesh and blood, relatives.
And that's why Jesus said that the first condition for discipleship,
Luke 1426, was to hate father, mother, brother, sister, wife, and children.
In other words, if I don't pour out that human attachment and soulish love for
my loved ones, I will not be able to love them wisely with a divine love.
And that is Paul's prayer for these Christians in Philippi.
Not that they will love one another with a soulish human attachment, but with a
divine love which seeks the best for the other, which has no other motive but the
glory of God.
And so he says, I pray that your love may abound in that way, in real knowledge
of God, in all discernment between soul and spirit, so that you may
distinguish between the things that differ and approve the things that are
excellent above the things that are merely good.
So that you may be finally sincere and blameless until the day of Christ.
This is how we can keep ourselves sincere and blameless until the day of Christ, as
we keep ourselves in love, irrespective of how the other person treats us.
One of the characteristics of divine love is that it has got nothing to do with the
way the other person treats you.
Human love waxes and wanes depending on how the other person responds,
and the other person responds positively in love to you, then you continue in love.
But if he cools off or he does something to hurt you, your love drops.
Now, that's the characteristic of human love, and we are to distinguish between
that type of love, which is merely human, and the type of love which is divine,
which has got nothing to do with the other person's response or reaction or
treatment of you.
And we are to partake of the divine nature which will make us sincere and
blameless.
Divine nature, which is love, is independent of the reactions of other people, and thus
we keep ourselves in love, sincere and blameless, until the day of Christ, having
been filled with the fruit of righteousness which comes through Jesus Christ to the glory
and praise of God.
Now, righteousness in the New Testament is essentially the same thing as love, for
Jesus said that the whole commandment hung upon these two basically, all the commandments
that Moses gave, hung upon basically these two commandments, both relating to love.
First, that you are to love God with all your heart, soul, and mind, and strength.
And second, you are to love your neighbor as yourself.
And the righteousness of the law is fulfilled when a person fulfills this commandment of
love.
And so the righteousness spoken of here is a righteousness of love.
And so when he says, having been filled with the fruit of righteousness, verse 11, he's
saying this is the fruit of righteousness that is to be manifested in your life.
If you say that you have been justified by faith in Christ, you've been declared
righteous, and that righteousness of Christ has been imputed to you, and now you are
partaking of the Holy Spirit's power so that that righteousness is manifested through
your life, then this is going to be the fruit.
What is it?
A love that abounds more and more towards our fellow believers, a love that approves
the things that are excellent and seeks the highest good of the other person.
Where a person is not growing in this type of love, he does not have the fruit of righteousness
that God seeks.
And so this is Paul's prayer for them.
How do we pray when we pray for other Christians?
Paul did not pray for other Christians that they would get better jobs and better houses
to live in and advance in this world.
Never once do we find him praying for these things.
If you see the prayers of Paul in the Epistles, you find he was always praying for some spiritual
advancement, some new revelation of the love of God for these people.
His prayers in Ephesians 1 and Ephesians 3, and here in Philippians 1-2, that people
may grow in fervent love for one another, approving the things that are excellent, discerning
between soul and spirit, and thus being filled with the fruit of righteousness which comes
through Jesus Christ.
It is not produced through our own strength, but through the part of Christ, and it is
not for our own glory.
Verse 11, it says, to the glory and praise of God alone.
We turn now to Philippians 1 and verse 12.
Now I want you to know, brethren, that my circumstances have turned out for the greater
progress of the gospel, so that my imprisonment and the cause of Christ has become well known
throughout the whole praetorian God and to everyone else, and that most of the brethren
trusting in the Lord because of my imprisonment have far more courage to speak the word of
God without fear.
Some to be sure are preaching Christ even from envy and strife, some also from good
will.
The latter do it out of love, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the gospel,
the former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, rather than from pure motives, thinking
to cause me distress in my imprisonment.
What then?
Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in
this I rejoice, yes, and I will rejoice.
For I know that this shall turn out for my deliverance through your prayers and the
provision of the spirit of Jesus Christ.
Now, one of the things that Paul makes very clear here is that he was a master of
circumstances.
We spoke in our first study on Philippians that one of the things that comes through
in this letter is Paul's triumphant joy.
He was in prison and he was rejoicing, and the Philippians also had heard of the
time when he was in prison in Philippi.
The jailer certainly heard him rejoicing there and praising God, and that's the time
the jailer was converted.
And so Paul could speak, having manifested that life before them, rejoicing the Lord
always, whether you're in prison or anywhere, and he was triumphant in every
circumstance.
He made every circumstance his servant.
And so he says in verse 12, I want you to know, brethren, that my circumstances
have turned out for the great progress of the gospel.
He had been imprisoned, and humanly speaking, one would have thought,
oh, what a sad thing, the great apostle has been locked up in jail.
And that would hinder the work of the gospel, for this apostle was one who
traveled much, but now he's locked up in jail how much God's work is hindered.
But God's ways are not our ways.
His ways of working are quite different from ours, and he says that these
circumstances which men would have thought would have hindered the progress of the
gospel have actually turned out for the furtherance of the gospel.
And this has happened in a number of ways.
First of all, verse 13, my imprisonment in the cause of Christ has become well
known throughout the whole praetorian God and to everyone else.
Throughout the palace of the governor, among the soldiers, it became well known
that Paul had been imprisoned for the cause of Christ.
Now, the way prisoners were locked up in those days, particularly those who were charged with
serious crimes like Paul was for preaching the gospel, was that they would be chained
together to a Roman soldier, and they would have to sit together for a number of hours.
Then perhaps four or six hours later, another soldier would come and take place of the
one who was chained together with Paul, and like that there would be a rotation in a day
of four to six soldiers who would be tied up to Paul.
And Paul used the opportunity to proclaim the gospel to each one of these soldiers who came
and were chained to him.
He had a captive audience.
There was a soldier chained to him, and Paul could share with him about the salvation
in Christ, and some of them opened their hearts and received Christ.
And so you find that just like Paul's imprisonment in Philippi turned out to the conversion of
the jailer there, Paul's imprisonment in Rome turned out to the conversion of a number
of the soldiers who were chained to him, and thereby the gospel spread throughout that
Roman soldier's God, called the praetorian God.
And it became well known, not only there but to many others, and thus the cause of the
gospel spread.
And here was another result of Paul's imprisonment, that when Paul was imprisoned, verse 14 it
says, most of the brethren trusted in the Lord because of his imprisonment, and as a
result had far more courage to speak the word of God without fear.
Persecution has an amazing way of producing greater boldness, because God gives special
grace at such times in the hearts of Christians, and this is exactly what happened to many
of the Christians, that they began to proclaim the gospel with greater boldness, and without
any fear to many others.
People who were quite silent before, probably who were letting Paul do most of the preaching
and thanking God for the apostles who were traveling about, but when one apostle got
locked up in prison, then they began to realize their responsibility more and began to proclaim
the gospel themselves.
So in both ways, the imprisonment of Paul turned out to the furtherance of the gospel,
and there's one more way that Paul was not aware of at that particular time, and
which is not recorded here, and that is Paul found time to write most of his letters only
when he was in prison.
Most of the rest of the time when he was free, he was traveling about preaching the gospel,
and wherever he went, he would work as a tentmaker and earn his own living, and the
result was that he had very little time really to sit down and write any letters.
Like we have in the Bible, Ephesians, Philippians, and many of the other letters that were written
in prison, and so we find that Paul's imprisonment became the cause of the writing of much of
the New Testament scriptures, and so we have much to thank God for, that Paul was
imprisoned.
If he had not been imprisoned, it's unlikely that he would have taken the time to sit down
and write these letters.
So God knew how best to bring forth in written form all that Paul had received and had been
revealed to him, and how it could be preserved through succeeding generations.
And so we see that even imprisonment works out the furtherance of God's purpose.
Now this is something that we need to remember, that all circumstances work together for
good to those who love God and who are called according to His purpose.
Now Paul was one who loved God and was called according to His purpose, and so everything
